summary: Many end-user sites still run mostly on IPv4 internally, but their devices increasingly need at least basic IPv6 as IPv6-only services appear. This informational document gives operational guidance for deploying IPv6 in such IPv4 sites using the Intra-Site Automatic Tunnel Addressing Protocol (ISATAP).

eli5.summary: An old-style network can carry new-style traffic through tunnels. This is advice for setting that up without rebuilding everything.

questions: ipv6 in ipv4-only sites using isatap
shared prefix vs individual prefix model
subtitle: Practical guidance for deploying IPv6 in IPv4-dominant enterprise networks using automatic tunneling.

tldr.problem: Many organizations still run IPv4 internally but increasingly need IPv6 connectivity as IPv6-only services emerge. Direct infrastructure replacement is costly and disruptive.
tldr.mechanism: ISATAP (Intra-Site Automatic Tunnel Addressing Protocol) encapsulates IPv6 in IPv4, letting hosts tunnel packets through existing IPv4 networks to ISATAP routers that connect to IPv6 Internet.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can add IPv6 services with minimal disruption by using existing IPv4 infrastructure as a transport layer. However, this is a transitional approach, not a long-term solution as native IPv6 deployment is eventually necessary.

facts.label: Address embedding
facts.value: IPv4 address embedded in IPv6 address

today: RFC 6964 is Informational status. ISATAP remains a practical transitional technology for enterprises deploying IPv6 alongside IPv4 infrastructure. It is not obsoleted by any other RFC, but native IPv6 deployment is the long-term goal as IPv4 becomes less common.

sections.title: IPv6 Deployment in IPv4 Networks
sections.content:
Most enterprise networks, from home offices to large corporations, have built their infrastructure around IPv4. These networks include firewalls, switches, routing systems, and countless devices all configured for IPv4. As IPv6-only services become more common on the Internet, internal devices need at least basic IPv6 capability to reach them. Rather than completely rebuilding networks from scratch, organizations can use ISATAP to add IPv6 support while leaving existing IPv4 infrastructure untouched.

The RFC provides operational guidance—real-world deployment advice—based on practical experience. It covers how to plan deployments, configure routers and hosts, handle multiple sites, manage address changes, and deal with technical issues like packet size constraints.
sections.eli5: Old companies have working IPv4 networks. Now they need IPv6 too. Instead of replacing everything, they can use a tunnel to run IPv6 through the old system.

sections.title: How ISATAP Works
sections.content:
ISATAP operates by encapsulating IPv6 packets inside IPv4 packets—a tunnel through the IPv4 network. Two types of nodes are involved: advertising routers (servers) and ISATAP hosts (clients). Routers advertise IPv6 prefixes and handle traffic between the ISATAP tunnel and the IPv6 Internet. Hosts automatically discover these routers, obtain IPv6 addresses using stateless autoconfiguration (SLAAC), and tunnel their IPv6 traffic to the routers.

The key insight is that ISATAP reuses existing IPv4 addresses to create IPv6 addresses. A host with IPv4 address 192.0.2.18 gets an IPv6 address like 2001:db8::5efe:192.0.2.18, embedding its IPv4 address in the IPv6 address itself. This allows routers to statelessly forward traffic: when an IPv6 packet arrives, the router can extract the destination host's IPv4 address from the destination IPv6 address.
sections.eli5: ISATAP wraps IPv6 packets in IPv4 packets, like putting letters in envelopes. The router reads an IPv6 address that contains the destination's IPv4 address, and knows exactly where to forward it.

sections.title: Two Deployment Models
sections.content:
ISATAP supports two main architectural approaches: the shared prefix model and the individual prefix model. In the shared model, all ISATAP routers advertise the same IPv6 prefix (e.g., 2001:db8::/64). This simplifies administration but requires routers to maintain detailed routing information about which addresses belong to which hosts. In the individual model, each router advertises its own unique prefix (e.g., router A advertises 2001:db8:0:1::/64, router B advertises 2001:db8:0:2::/64). This distributes knowledge more cleanly: IPv6 routing naturally directs traffic to the correct router based on the prefix.

The choice depends on site topology. Small networks or centralized architectures favor the shared model. Large networks with multiple independent segments favor the individual model. Sites can also mix both models in different parts of the network.
sections.eli5: Shared model: one address block, all routers advertise it, routers must track who is who. Individual model: each router has its own address block, traffic finds the right router automatically.

sections.title: Planning and Managing ISATAP Deployments
sections.content:
Successful ISATAP deployment requires careful administration. Site administrators must plan address allocation so that IPv6 prefix boundaries align with IPv4 subnet boundaries; this enables simpler routing and filtering. They should configure access control lists to handle interface identifier compatibility—some legacy devices set identification bits differently. Site administrators can control host address selection policies to prefer IPv4 for internal communication (avoiding tunnel overhead) while using IPv6 for external services.

When the site later renumbers to a new ISP-supplied IPv6 prefix, ISATAP makes this straightforward: routers simply begin advertising new prefixes, and hosts' addresses automatically expire and renew with fresh prefixes. For sites with multiple partitions (like different office buildings), administrators must configure routers to exchange routing information, ensuring traffic reaches the correct partition.
sections.eli5: Administrators must decide how to allocate addresses, configure routers to talk to each other, and set up rules for when hosts should use IPv4 versus IPv6. When moving to a new ISP, the old addresses naturally expire and new ones appear.

sections.title: Scaling, Path MTU, and Alternatives
sections.content:
ISATAP can scale to larger networks by deploying additional routers and forming a mesh or hub-and-spoke topology where routers coordinate using IPv6 routing protocols. Each router distributes prefixes appropriately to balance traffic and ensure redundancy.

A technical constraint is Path MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit): IPv6-in-IPv4 encapsulation adds overhead, reducing the effective packet size. The RFC recommends the "dynamic" method for MTU discovery in well-managed networks, which can achieve better throughput than conservative static limits.

The RFC also notes that other approaches exist: 6rd (IPv6 Rapid Deployment) offers stateless delegation; tunnel brokers provide point-to-point tunnels; 6to4 and Teredo offer less-managed alternatives. ISATAP's advantage is that it works cleanly within a single administrative domain without requiring external services.
sections.eli5: For bigger sites, add more routers that share information. Wrapped packets are slightly smaller than pure IPv6 packets, so networks should use proper methods to measure safe packet sizes. Other tunneling technologies exist but ISATAP fits organizations without needing outside help.

sections.title: Security and Deployment Assurance
sections.content:
ISATAP inherits security considerations from the underlying IPv6 and IP tunneling specs. The main operational security concern is routing loops: if an advertising ISATAP router receives a packet that would be forwarded back to itself, it can create a loop. The RFC advises administrators to configure routers to drop such packets. Additionally, sites should prevent tunneled packets from looping back to the same router.

The technology is deployable in existing well-managed enterprise networks today, as it requires only software configuration on routers and hosts—no new hardware. Since the RFC is informational, not a standard, operators should consult RFC 5214 (the ISATAP specification) and related RFCs on tunneling security for complete details.
sections.eli5: The main risk is packets bouncing back and forth between routers forever. Administrators configure routers to prevent this. ISATAP is ready to use now in managed enterprise environments.
